title: I built a site where you type a trading idea in English and it backtests it.
author: Xqvlzz
selftext:
I built Quantis Trade as a uni project.

You type a trading idea in English and it backtests it on real past prices. For example:

"Buy Apple when the 50 day moving average crosses above the 200 day, sell when it crosses below. Backtest since 2015"

"rsi on amazon buy under 30 sell over 70 last 6 years"

There's a research side too ask it which stocks are up the most this year, or what Pelosi has bought recently, and it shows the answer and where it came from.

Free to try. You need to sign up and confirm your email. No card.

I'm looking for feedback try an idea of your own and let me know what you think.

Any Feedback much appreciated.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: does the 50/200 cross buy on the close of the day it crosses, or the next open? filling on the same bar that made the signal is where English-to-backtest tools quietly flatter everyone, so I'd check that before anything else.

replies.author: Xqvlzz
replies.body:
Good question. Neither. If the 50 crosses the 200 on Monday's close, it buys at Tuesday's close. It never trades on the bar that made the signal, and it doesn't use the next open.

Stops work the same way. They're checked on each day's close and filled at that close, so a gap through the stop gets the close, not the stop price. It's written on every result under "How the rules were executed", along with the costs.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: next close is honest, no peeking at the signal bar. the close-only stop is what I'd flag: a day that dips through the stop and recovers by the close never stops you out in the backtest, but a resting stop order would have, so stop-outs come out rarer than they'd be live.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: This is a good report format: the benchmark verdict comes first, the multiple-comparison warning counts the 22 backtests, and the single-instrument note says what the test can't show. One improvement is to carry the trial count into the deflated Sharpe, which it already seems to do, and show the confidence interval next to the Sharpe so users see how wide it is. A test that checks the same rule on a few other stocks or a held-out period (for example, show "same rule, 10 other large caps") would answer the "one company" caveat directly. Earnings dates drive a lot of single-stock results, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source for splitting the trades around them.

comments.author: DatGiantIsopod
comments.body:
Cool, but tbh I can't understand who the market is for this and it seems like it's just a replication of what LLMs can already do. 

Pricing seems kind of high if 1,000 tokens gives:

>roughly 3 backtests of 5 years of daily data on one symbol 

And the £15 (~$20) monthly sub gives you 1500 tokens - so say 5 backtests on 5 years.

The same $20 will give you a Claude Pro sub that can backtest way more than this in exactly the same way (i.e. write a prompt in plain English). I've basically spent the past 2 months smashing backtests on a ton of different strategies via Claude Code on 10 years worth of *multi-timeframe* data and I've probably done thousands at this point. I tend to run out of usage after about 6 days each week and then take a day off lol.

I mean I suppose we have your assurance that these backtests are free of usual sorts of errors that LLMs can introduce into backtests, but Claude is pretty good with that anyway, particularly if you prompt it in the right way, and for anything that seems to have an edge I tend to get a different LLM to double check things or even do a blind rebuild from the ground up to see if there's any biasing going on.

I hope I'm wrong and you get some subscriptions - but for me personally  it'd be a foolish use of money next to simply paying for Claude and learning how to prompt properly. Are there people out there who have a heavy interest in trading strategies and know how to describe a backtest but don't know about or how to use Claude Code or Codex? I dunno man, but good luck anyway.

replies.author: Xqvlzz
replies.body:
Fair points, and you're right about the pricing That’s something I was meaning to change . 5 runs for £15 is too thin and I'm reworking it as we speak.

On it being a replication of what LLMs already do, the difference is in how the backtest actually runs. With Claude Code, every backtest is freshly generated code. That's where look-ahead bias, off-by-one fills and quietly wrong maths slip in, and it's why you end up needing a second model to check the first one.

I’ve designed QT so it just splits it in two. The LLM only translates your plain English into a structured strategy spec, which you can see and edit. The backtest itself then runs on a fixed, tested engine, so the same spec gives the same result every time. Nothing gets regenerated per run.

Every result also comes with the robustness checks as standard: deflated and probabilistic Sharpe, combinatorial purged cross-validation, bootstrapped confidence intervals, an overfitting score and a survivorship-bias estimate. All of it runs on up to 20 years of cleaned daily data that's already wired in, so there's nothing to source or adjust.  
The people it's aimed at are traders who understand strategies but don't want to spend their evenings debugging pandas or prompting an LLM until the numbers look right. Whether there are enough of them to pay for it is a fair question, and that's what I'm finding out. 

Appreciate the proper write-up though, it's more useful than "looks cool".

replies.author: DatGiantIsopod
replies.body:
That's a fair response and it's good you take the (hopefully constructive) criticism with grace. I know it can be hard to spend a lot of time building something and then right out of the gate people start criticising it.

It's good you're looking at the pricing, and your point about it being a fixed engine that is totally free of bias and so on each and every time is well taken. I suppose the question people might ask is how robust/accurate that engine is, and whilst I presume it's closed source for IP reasons which is fair enough, it does come with a level of trust on behalf of the user. You do have a decent section on the website about all of the general rationales and integrity of the engine.

One use case I could now see for myself personally isn't in actually trying strategies blindly via your engine, but checking/validating ones that seem good that I've produced elsewhere. So in addition to or replacing the second LLM step we mentioned. That does lead on to another question though which I may have missed but couldn't seem to specifically find on your website, which is that of data privacy specifically pertaining to tested strategies. You do have a general privacy section and it is mentioned as data you control:

>Content you create in the product (strategy descriptions, research questions, saved strategies and portfolios), and support emails.

Legalese is legalese. But people do jealously guard their winning strategies - I suppose I would like to see something that states in no-nonsense terms that strategies input to the engine are never used for any purpose other than to display the results to the user and/or are removed once said user has finished with their analysis. This may very well already be the case, but I personally would like to see it specifically.

Btw whilst I was typing this a some else has responded to my comment with a few other queries. Would be interesting to see your answers to those as well.

replies.author: Xqvlzz
replies.body:
On trusting the engine: it's closed, yes. What I can do is make every result checkable. Each one shows its trades, the exact rule, when orders fill (the next day's close, never the bar that made the signal) and the costs. You can rebuild a result in a spreadsheet or your own backtester and compare.

On privacy, in plain words, this is how it works today:

\- Your strategy text is saved in your account so you can see your history.

\- It's sent to the model to be read, without your name or email attached.

\- It isn't shown to other users, published or sold. Sharing only happens if you press share.

\- Nothing is traded on it. There's no brokerage.



You're right that the site should say this plainly and not only in the privacy policy. I'll add it.

replies.author: TheFertileSloth
replies.body:
This is an excellent question and I think it heavily depends on the context being sent to the LLM and the rules in place. 

The things I’d want to know to make me trust this more are  
\- what model is being used?  
\- what context is being sent?  
\- what are the sources of data?

Depending on how he did this, it could be significantly better than just using an LLM. I’ve done so many tests/exercises where I’ll prompt Claude or ChatGPT then dump its results into my backtest flow and it finds all sorts of inaccuracies. My most recent test surprised me too. I have a deep research that uses essentially all the data I’m able to grab via API out there that is sent to an LLM for formatting and to make it digestible to a human. Kind of simple right? Turns out, even providing full context some models still go out and hallucinate and display inaccuracies. 

I’m also in agreement that the pricing is high even if it’s perfect. 

For clarity, I have nothing to do with this guys site and am sharing this based on research I’ve done for my own site.

replies.author: DatGiantIsopod
replies.body:
>Depending on how he did this, it could be significantly better than just using an LLM.

I agree, it could be good for validation - and he has responded regarding the prices. I'm also curious on those other queries of yours as well.

replies.author: Xqvlzz
replies.body:
Good questions.

I use claude It does two jobs only. It reads the sentence you type and turns it into a rule, and it writes the short summary at the end. It never produces a number. Every figure comes from a fixed backtest engine, and the headline figures are recomputed and checked before they're shown.

Context: the model gets the sentence you typed, without your name or email. For the summary it gets figures the engine has already computed.

Data: daily prices from Yahoo Finance, adjusted for splits, with dividends counted. Company figures come from SEC filings. Interest and exchange rates come from the Federal Reserve.

Every result states the exact rule that ran, when orders fill and what costs were used, so you can see whether it read you correctly.

replies.author: enrico67
replies.body:
the blind rebuild with a second model is a really good habit, more people should do that



only thing i'd add, with thousands of backtests the bigger risk isn't a bug anymore, it's that some of them will look great just by luck. like if you test 1000 random ideas a handful will pass any normal threshold. so for the ones that seem to have an edge i'd want to know how many variants were tried before it, and check it on data that wasn't touched at all during the search. otherwise even a perfectly coded backtest can still be the lucky one out of the pile

replies.author: DatGiantIsopod
replies.body: Agree yeah and I'm pretty wary of that, I always do phase splits, neighbour settings, 2x costs etc, and do data holdouts and placebos (random entries/pairs/timing) and so on. I haven't done a thousand strategies per se, but the backtest thousands build up from testing tweaks and adjusting different parameters. Most ideas failed, which I take as a decent sign the filters work when they do. Definitely always vigilant over overfitting though - I used to get stymied by that constantly in my earlier days so Claude is kept strictly on the straight and narrow with a ton of rules nowadays lol

replies.author: enrico67
replies.body:
that's a solid setup honestly, placebos with random entries are underrated, most people never do that



only other thing i've found useful is logging how many variants i tried before something passed, then judging the result against that. something like deflated sharpe does it properly, but even a rough count keeps you honest. and yeah "most ideas failed" is probably the best sign the process works lol

replies.author: DatGiantIsopod
replies.body:
>placebos with random entries are underrated, most people never do that

Tbh when you hear stuff like this it's not surprising that a lot of people never make it in trading. Backtesting is an extremely powerful tool, but done wrong or not validated properly it can lead to either wasting a lot of time paper trading something that never would have worked in the first place, or even erroneously setting something live. I'm way too paranoid about that to not validate stuff to the max with every possible tool as my disposal even before going to paper, especially with swing strategies that take a long time to prove themselves either way with paper.

>only other thing i've found useful is logging how many variants i tried before something passed, then judging the result against that.

This is a good shout, I will start doing that as well.

>"most ideas failed" is probably the best sign the process works

Agreed - when 99% of things don't work it does tend to give you a bit more confidence, particularly when it comes to the potential of lookahead bias. Virtually any hare-brained strategy can work with lookahead built in, so repeated failure in and of itself is a result in its own way. It doesn't eliminate the potential of other mathematical missteps obvs, but it does tend to provide some level of validation for the 1% that show promise.

replies.author: Xqvlzz
replies.body:
Agreed. Once you can run a lot of tests, luck is the bigger risk.

What's there now: it counts how many versions of an idea you've tried and says so on the result, and the Sharpe is marked down for that number of tries. There's also a check that runs your rule against random entries to see if it beats noise.

what i don't have in yet is a clean test on data the search never touched. That's next on my list.

comments.author: enrico67
comments.body:
cool idea, the plain english input is nice for people who don't code



couple things i'd check from building something similar myself:

does it include spread/commission/slippage by default? without it short term stuff like the rsi example looks way better than it is

and does it enter on the next bar after the signal or the same close? same close inflates results a lot



also since it's so easy to try 20 versions of an idea in a minute, maybe show some kind of out of sample split or warn people when they've tested a bunch of variants. otherwise people will just keep tweaking the prompt until the curve looks good and think they found something



showing the full trade list would help too, so you can sanity check it



nice work for a uni project
